transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
- Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Linda Kenyon.
Stocks opened mixed this morning
and remain mixed at the moment after big gains yesterday.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports the Dow Jones industrial average
rose about 150 points in early trading.
- Invidia shares opened down,
reversing a fraction of the previous day's gain.
Stock and the chipmaker soared more than 30% on Monday,
following the return of CEO Jensen Wong.
President Trump took credit for Wong's reinstatement,
saying he'd personally lobbied the Invidia board.
The broader market also rallied on Monday,
although doubts remain about the staying power
of the artificial intelligence boom.
Shares of AI powerhouse anthropic
opened below last week's IPO price.
A couple of big retailers
offered better than expected earnings reports.
Best Buy notched its best sales growth in years,
and Dick's sporting goods scored with an upbeat outlook.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
- Invidia's board brought Jensen Wong back
less than two weeks after he resigned,
and many Silicon Valley CEOs and investors
are welcoming his reinstatement.
NPR's Shannon Bond reports.
- SpaceX CEO Elon Musk posted on social media,
quote, "The mistake has been corrected."
Gavin Baker, whose firm Invest in Invidia,
posted a video of employees cheering and clapping for Wong
at the chipmaker's headquarters.
Tech historian Margaret O'Mara says the reaction reflects
Silicon Valley's reverence for founders.
- It's the argument made by a lot in Silicon Valley
last week, and by the president,
that Invidia's success depends on Jensen running it.
- Many tech leaders have loudly called for Wong's return,
even as questions remain about reports
the Invidia founder had an affair
with a woman U.S. officials
suspected of working with Chinese intelligence.
Shannon Bond, NPR News.
- The U.S. Army confirms it will proceed with its plans
to detonate nearly five tons of bomb-making material
in eastern Iowa tomorrow.
Now that a federal appeals court has denied a request
to stop it, Eliza Billingham from Iowa Public Radio reports.
- Some residents near the Iowa Army ammunition plant
in Middletown, Iowa are concerned about toxic lead-laden dust
from the explosion.
Those same worries prompted a lawsuit from environmentalists
seeking to stop the detonation,
but the court ruled in favor of the Army
saying the risks from the control detonation are lower
than the risks of other disposal strategies,
or doing nothing, in which case the material
is likely to explode on its own.
Mayor of Middletown Rodney Johnson said earlier this week.
- Let's stop the fair mongering
and get rid of this highly explosive material
once and for all.
- The Army says cold weather
makes lead azide even more volatile,
which makes the situation that much more urgent.
For NPR News, I'm Eliza Billingham in Iowa City.
- On Wall Street right now,
the Dow is up more than 251 points,
the S&P 500, Dow 23.
You're listening to NPR.
As Americans gather to celebrate Thanksgiving,
experts recommend following a few key food safety tips
to keep foodborne illness away from your holiday table.
NPR's Maria Godoy has some useful tips
for those of us who are preparing the Thanksgiving dinner.
First, keep a clean kitchen.
Wash your hands before preparing food,
clean and sanitized surfaces, and cutting boards,
and make sure to keep raw meat
separate from foods that don't get cooked,
such as salad vegetables and breads.
If you use a cutting board for raw meat,
make sure to put it in the sink
so no one else accidentally uses it for other foods.
If you're cooking turkey,
it should reach an internal temperature of 165 degrees
to kill harmful bacteria,
says David Love of Johns Hopkins University.
- So I like to keep a meat thermometer handy,
and that's a great way to tell when your meal's done.
- He says, "Chill any leftovers in the fridge or cooler
within two hours of serving to prevent the growth of bacteria."
Maria Godoy, NPR News.
- A Pakistani man is said to become
the first foreign astronaut to board China's space station.
China introduced the crew to reporters
ahead of this week's launch.
Pakistani astronaut Mohammed Zishan Ali
will join two Chinese astronauts for this mission,
which will launch tomorrow morning.
Ali previously served as an Air Force pilot.
Speaking at a news conference,
he thanked the Chinese government
for helping him make his dream come true.
- I'm Linda Kenyon, NPR News in Washington.
